The biggest difference is in their conviction.

Capitalists have had steadily increasing conviction levels over the last two years... over the same time horizon the Fundamentalists have had steadily declining conviction.

US commercial crude oil inventories are reaching critical levels:

Crude inventories at Cushing, Oklahoma, the largest commercial storage hub in the US and the pricing point for WTI Crude, dropped -1.6 million barrels last week, to 20 million barrels, the lowest since 2014.

This marks the 8th consecutive weekly decline, totaling -8.3 million barrels.

As a result, Cushing now holds less than 2 days worth of US crude production, approaching the minimum level at which the facility can continue pumping oil efficiently.

Once inventories fall below ~20 million barrels, extracting crude becomes technically difficult and more costly, while oil quality can deteriorate due to water and sediment.

Meanwhile, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve is down to ~340 million barrels, the lowest since 1983, after 172 million barrels were released to contain war-driven fuel price increases.

US oil inventories down to levels rarely seen in modern energy markets.

Between 2003 and 2024, Berkshire’s P&C insurance subsidiaries cumulatively generated $36 billion in underwriting profit.
In 2024 alone, Ajit Jain disclosed at the annual meeting, Berkshire earned a 2.2% underwriting profit on its float. That is a 2.2% yield, on $170 billion, roughly $3.7 billion of profit before Berkshire earned a single dollar of investment return.
Buffett’s genius was not merely picking good stocks. That was the relatively easy part. Buffett’s genius was in building an insurance company that generated free capital and then not blowing up the underwriting in the pursuit of growth.
Every competitor in the P&C industry eventually succumbs to the temptation to write more policies at cheaper rates to grow the top line. Buffett built a culture that did the opposite: in hard markets Berkshire wrote aggressively, in soft markets Berkshire walked away. Insurance volumes at Berkshire have declined in some years — voluntarily — because the pricing was not attractive. 
That discipline is Berkshire's most valuable edge. And it is the piece of the Berkshire's culture that worries me most about the post-Buffett transition. Greg Abel did not build the insurance discipline. Ajit Jain did, and Tony Nicely did, and a generation of Berkshire underwriters who learned the culture at Buffett’s elbow. When they go, the discipline may go with them. That is the risk nobody at Berkshire is discussing publicly, but it is, by far, the single biggest risk to the enterprise.

America’s standard of living has been in decline for decades.

There is a group of respected intellectuals — Charles Murray, Nicholas Eberstadt, Robert Putnam, and to some degree J.D. Vance — who paint the story of America’s decline as a failure of culture. In these narratives, we are in trouble because we abandoned the habits of thrift, work, and family formation. As a consequence, America’s families and economic lives are falling apart. The failure is in the souls of Americans, and the remedy is a moral reconstruction.

I have enormous respect for these writers. I think they are describing, with real precision, the sociological texture of what has happened. But I know they have the causation backward.

In America’s ongoing decline, the social scientists are adept at measuring the obvious signs of distress: drug addiction, gambling, prostitution, suicide. But these problems did not destroy our culture. These problems are a result of what has been destroying our country. And that is hard for them to measure because they are not looking at the economics behind these changes.

A culture of thrift does not survive a monetary regime that punishes savers.
A culture of marriage does not survive an economy in which young men cannot afford to form households.
A culture of work does not survive a labor market in which working-class wages have tracked sideways for 50 years while asset prices have gone to the moon.

The cultural problems — the lack of thrift, the abandonment of marriage, and chronic underemployment — are rational responses to our current economic environment. When the economy ceases to reward traditional male roles, the culture adjusts. 

You can see this clearly if you look at the exceptions. 

In every demographic slice of America where the Cantillon transfer has been positive — where the households in question have been recipients of the new money, not victims of it — the old cultural patterns are completely intact.

Upper-middle-class professionals in Bethesda still marry at high rates. They still form stable families. They still raise their children with discipline, invest in their education, attend their kids’ sporting events, and stay married into their seventies.

They did not suffer a cultural collapse, because they did not suffer an economic collapse.

It is the people who did not receive the new money whose culture has come apart. And that is not a coincidence. That is the causation.

If you want to rebuild America’s culture, you have to first rebuild the currency.
